utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, good morning. May we continue where we left off yesterday. I hope we weren't going on for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to have document Z908/1, and perhaps to speed things up perhaps another document, Z903, 963.1, and 1226.1. If they could all be on the witness's table so that we could get through them quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the documents, General, may I just remind you that the first document we're going to look at is the information about the joint command for Central Bosnia and the headquarters for Vitez, the joint commission for Vitez, as UNPROFOR refers to it. 908.1, please is the first document, Z980.1. This one here. You have already seen the document. It was on the table before you several times. It contains the names from both sides of people delegated and appointed to the joint command. We discussed this -- there were discussions on this before these proposals were finally defined, and there was a general position taken at different meetings that the two sides should put forward officers to become members of this joint command who had not been compromised in conflicts up to that time, particularly not in the ethnic sense, not ethnically compromised. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. No. That was not a subject discussed at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So according to you, conditions were not laid down -- I use the term "conditions" in a broad sense -- as to which individual should become a part, a member of this joint command?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. There was no discussion about that. We accepted the proposals put forward by the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as we're talking about the Vitez joint commission, do you agree that this included Mario Cerkez, and although the time isn't -- the correct date isn't quoted, and Marijan Skopljak, which says -- and for him it says "Chief of Defence of Vitez." Can you confirm that these two names were in this joint command from the Vitez side?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The joint command was located in the post office in Travnik, and the local joint commissions were established at the level of the municipalities and brigades. At meetings of a local level, Mario Cerkez would come to those meetings, and I think Marijan Skopljak was there too, but I remember that Mario Cerkez was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So we can agree that these were the names in these commissions.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And that is how co-operation started. And we're only talking about the Vitez level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you please now take a look at document Z903, 903, and take a look at the last page and the signatures on that page. It says "Cerkez" and "Kalestura". And from this order on the 11th of May, that is to say, soon after this commission was established, I think it was on the following day, in fact, this joint commission, the Cerkez/Kalestura one, set up a commission, and it stipulates the names of the members of that commission, to deal with outstanding questions, and there we have them liberating the prisoners, the state of the wounded, and so on and so forth. First of all, can we agree that these four names of members of the commission are two from the Croatian side and two from the Muslim side; that is to say, from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That commission started work, did it not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Meetings were organised at which we had Mr. Franjo Nakic and myself from the joint commission, and there were meetings at a local level, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we can agree -- let us try and be as brief as possible, without any comments when they're not necessary -- the commission started functioning. And do you agree that it did get through a very serious and difficult piece of business?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The commission worked on the ground. Whether it functioned as is stated in the document, I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But can you confirm that it worked diligently?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For illustration purposes, we have another document compiled by the commission later in the course of its work, and it was Z965.1. That is that particular document. And if we take a look at the signatures on that document, you will agree that that is the commission in question, is it not, from the previous order?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when we read this document, although it is self-explanatory, so we don't have to waste time on it, but we can see that on the basis of their work, they give an explanation of the competencies of the work of the commission. Do you agree that that is that particular commission?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I do agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that we can see that the joint commission was, in fact, functioning?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The joint commission worked on the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Have you had occasion to see other reports compiled by that commission during that period?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There were reports, but I cannot say at the moment what the reports actually were because it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. You can put down those documents. We have finished looking into them. At one point of your testimony, I think it was on the first day of your testimony, you said that on the 15th of April, on the road from Vitez towards Zenica, you saw somewhere at Kaonik, on the road by the Sunce Cafe, that you saw 30 to 50 HVO soldiers wearing black uniforms; that they had rallied around that particular establishment. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, that particular locality, in view of your knowledge of the area, do you agree that it was outside the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us move on. Further in your testimony you stated that the village guards were not under the control of the BiH army. And I'd like to ask you two or three questions for clarification purposes in that regard. Do you consider that the village guards were self-organised?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At the level of the village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the level of the village. I see. And above that level it was the Territorial Defence, was it not, which tried to place the village guards under its control, and I am talking about the Territorial Defence which was controlled by the Muslim side, at least in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence never dealt with the question of village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the initiative to organise village guards, and we are talking about both sides, the Croatian and the Muslim side, was that initiative taken by the sides themselves, the parties?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I cannot say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And a direct question to wind up. According to your knowledge, and your opinion, who organised village guards in the course of 1992? Who was it who organised them?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I assume that they were organised by the villages themselves, in view of the crime that took place and was prevalent during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the villages themselves, to protect themselves from any criminals on the lurch?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, please, the village guards, at least in a considerable number of villages, and in the Vitez area, I don't know outside this area, but they were mixed, were they not, mixed in composition; that is to say, all the villages, all the population of the villages organised these village guards, and that it was not only the Croats or the Muslims? I think you'll agree.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In some villages that is true, yes, but afterwards I think those village guards became a separate --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean on a national basis, nationality basis, ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about this, that there was a regrouping of these village guards, and then that they were dismantled, and then they met again, that is to say that these village guards reacted to current events taking place in their micro community?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that. I haven't got any information on that, but possibly that did happen on the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point in your testimony you stated that before April, 1993, the HVO had high calibre artillery and that you thought that it was located in the quarry in the Vitez area. And I have two or three questions for clarification purposes in that regard, in connection to the artillery. The BiH army in the broader area of Vitez, that is to say the Vitez municipality, also had artillery weapons; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, by saying what you've said, were you thinking about the howitzers of 152 and 122 millimetres which existed in the area? Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know what side you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am first asking whether the HVO had artillery of this calibre and category, howitzer 152 and 122.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, that it had these howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, do you recall that between the 3rd Corps and the operative zone, and we are talking about the time before April, 1993, and you mentioned this, that between these two commands, in order to support the front line at Vlasic, it was decided that each side should give one howitzer, which it did, and that two 152 howitzers were positioned in the quarry at Mosunj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We attempted, in the autumn of 1992, to establish a joint artillery, but that never came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you claim that there was never a pair of howitzers, a place there, each side providing one, and an agreement on giving support and reinforcement to Vlasic, between the operative zone and the 3rd Corps, that an agreement of that kind had been reached and that the effects of it were placed at the front lines there? Do you claim that that never took place?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We agreed that that should be so, but there was no use -- no use was reaped from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, and you are a military man, I am not, that looking at it from the aspects of utilisation and the justification for having this, the fact that this was at a distance of 125 kilometres to the front line at Vlasic, that this would have been an ideal position for placing artillery of this 152 and possibly 122 calibre weapons?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In the talks that we had, we proposed other positions for the artillery, but this was never accepted by the HVO, because the HVO deployed the artillery as it saw fit. It never took into account the proposals we made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me something else in this regard, General. The artillery of this type and this calibre, this power, it was evidently not intended for fighting in the -- around the narrow area where it was located. That is true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, because it is a long distance artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it was not required for the support and reinforcement of troops in the town of Vitez proper?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I don't agree with you there, because it depends where the artillery was deployed and positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that in principle it was long-range weaponry?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If you place long-range artillery far enough away from Vitez, it can be used to target Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Tell us, please, from the talks and agreements that you had, do you agree that this particular artillery of this calibre was under the control of the operative zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you answer that, General, as to who the artillery on the other side was under the command of? Or is it something that you can only speculate upon?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know who was in command of that artillery. I can only assume that the command -- it was the command of the artillery unit. But I don't know his name and surname. I don't know who was in command, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. Document Z1226,1. It is this milinfosum document. That's right. That's the one. I should like to draw your attention to the first, second, third paragraph. It is the third paragraph on that first page, and it is "CC Travnik," the title, and in brackets it has point 1, and it begins with the words "HCC met Mr. Merdan." I think we should have a translation of this document somewhere. Your Honours, I seem to have mixed something up, because this document was tendered by the Prosecution, and I thought we had a Croatian translation, but we don't. So let me take a little time to explain what it's about to the witness. I apologise, General, I thought you had a translation of the text. But in this excerpt, this excerpt mentions the talks between the representative of the ECMM with you, and in the last sentence of this paragraph it states that you spoke about, went on to speak about the efforts or attempts made by Mr. Abdic to establish an autonomous province in Western Bosnia, and that his endeavours were motivated by some personal, private expectations and gains. And that it was fated to failure. Tell us, please, who was Mr. Abdic, the Mr. Abdic that you mention here?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know what period you're thinking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is the period of the 30th of September, 1993. You spoke about the events at the time.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At that time, as far as I know, Fikret Abdic was located in Western Krajina. The Western Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That means the far western part of Bosnia, around the Bihac area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, is it the part of Bosnia, to avoid any misunderstanding, that is called Cazinska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the Cazinska Krajina area is located; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The people there of Cazin call it the Cazinska Krajina, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell us, there was a conflict there between the forces of Abdic, which he had recruited, and the BiH forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much about that. My colleague has just cautioned me, because we know a name but you do not know. Mr. Fikret Abdic is a Muslim by ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Furthermore, in your testimony, General, at one point you state that you had communications via Paket link, and I have just a brief question in that regard. Is that a sophisticated system of links or is it a primitive system of communication? At what level of the present technology, communications technology used in Bosnia? Where was this, at the top level, the lower level, at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At that time it was a top level, top quality communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean sophisticated?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time it was a sophisticated means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia also used this kind of link in respect to the other enclaves such as Kiseljak and Vares? Did you know that then or did you find out about that later?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The HVO had similar communications, and I think at that time the HVO had a more modern means of communication. It was better equipped than was the BiH army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, tell me, please, whether -- let me put it this way: A number of -- many numbers are mentioned when we speak of the numerical composition of the 3rd Corps during the summer of 1993. So for July or August. One figure mentioned, which seems to be realistic, is 20.000 soldiers of the 30th Corps -- I'm sorry, 3rd Corps in the summer of 1993. Is that correct? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but I think there were around 20.000 men, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will you please look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the usher assist me in distributing this document, please? [In English] It is Croatian text on the top and translation in English on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please be kind enough to look at the first two pages which are in Croatian, and the signature, the number, the date. General, can you confirm that this is the document issued by you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to read through the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, could I ask for the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D55/2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could a copy be placed under the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you, but let us know when you've read it.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, as a layman, I understand this to be preparations of the army for conflicts for a war and for a long winter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: What you are saying is correct, but I have a comment to make regarding this order. I always signed this as a Commandant, and the word zapovjednik is used, both meaning "commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you say this is not your document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This was drafted by my staff, and I did sign it. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we agree this was a circular letter to several commands, but this particular one is addressed to the command in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that this was addressed to the units that you mentioned yesterday, the parties of the 325th that were located in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then to some other unit?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: To municipal Territorial Defence staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Thank you. Just one more question, General. Yesterday, on a number of occasions, you mentioned the 3rd Corps, its structure. What about the 7th Corps, which was also operating in this area or, rather, from what date onwards was the 7th Corps present in the area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but there is an order in the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the exact date of the formation of the 7th Corps. It was established by a division of the 3rd Corps. A part of the forces of the 3rd Corps formed the 7th Corps, and it had a different zone of operations than the 3rd Corps. There was a division of the areas of operations between the two corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General, is it right that parts of the 7th Corps stayed on at places along lines bordering with the Lasva enclave or the Lasva Valley? Would it be correct to say that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is partly true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that around the whole enclave of the Lasva Valley covering the municipalities of Novi Travnik, Vitez, and Busovaca was surrounded by units of the 3rd Corps and later of the 7th Corps of the BH Army as well?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Prior to the formation of the 3rd Corps -- no, I'm sorry, the 7th Corps, units of the 3rd Corps were partly there. And after the 7th Corps was formed, units of the 7th Corps were partly there. I say "partly," because the bulk of the forces of the 3rd Corps and the 7th Corps were deployed toward the aggressor against Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So can we agree that this was roughly at the beginning of August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot confirm the date. So could we please check with the documents or the orders referring to this matter, and they can be found in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But let me put it in broader terms. We can agree that it was sometime in the summer, but we don't know the exact date. The summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, one further matter in this connection. Toward the end of the summer or, rather, the beginning of September, 1993, the personnel of the 3rd and the 7th Corps, or the part of the 7th Corps that was in the vicinity of the Lasva Valley, that is, BH Army forces located around the Lasva enclave or the Lasva Valley, were of some 30.000 strength?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you are referring to the number of inhabitants or the number of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The number of troops.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I do not agree with that estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You think there were fewer?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Certainly much fewer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That brings to an end my cross-examination. Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, a few questions. Some of them will be capable of very short answers. Tisovac, did you go there yourself? If so, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: During the conflicts, I didn't personally go to Tisovac, but I am very familiar with it, because I visited it several times prior to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In short, is it a fairly remote place in woodland near a fish farm?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is about four kilometres from Busovaca, and there was a fish farm there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us that after your arrest and beating, Glavocevic brought you words of apology. We know that Exhibit 100, which we haven't had to look at, was the warrant for your arrest signed by Kordic. At least we haven't had to look at it in detail for the arrest. Was anything said, by way of explanation for your arrest, or any apology for your arrest, when Florijan spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, no apologies were addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What indeed did he say on Kordic's behalf, when he came to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I cannot remember all the details, but he did say that he was sorry that it had happened and that it should not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No explanation for having you arrested in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, no explanation. I was not given any explanation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke of the man, Bruno Susnja. In a word, explain who he was and why you say he should be called to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Bruno Susnja is an inhabitant of Busovaca municipality, with whom I used to associate before the war. I know for sure that Bruno Susnja is the founder of the HDZ party in Busovaca. I think he was also the first president of that party for Busovaca municipality. I had several contacts with him, in the course of 1991. I think that he was a person with very realistic opinions regarding the danger that was looming of aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, something we discussed several times. I also talked to him in the course of 1992. I think that for a time he was influential among HDZ members. Later, he told me that all power had been taken over by Dario Kordic and that Dario Kordic was the alpha and omega not only of the HDZ in Busovaca, but further afield, and that he was the person making the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've spoken on several occasions of the HVO having control of any Arabs that entered the territory. Can you just explain whether there could be any advantage to the HVO in allowing Arabs in at that time, and if so, what advantage?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: May I go back briefly to the question of Bruno Susnja. I had another meeting with Bruno Susnja in Zenica, I recollect very well now, when he was fleeing from Dario Kordic, who, according to Bruno's allegation, had tried to kill him. And he fled to Zenica. Now, to come back to this other question that you put to me. I am still convinced that the HVO knew how many Arabs were entering Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was aware at the time that the Arabs brought money. I don't know how and from where. This was outside anyone's control. That they used very expensive vehicles and they were always stopped at HVO checkpoints, arrested, taken into custody and looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what, if any, advantage could there have been to the HVO in permitting them in at all?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In my statement I have already said that the kidnappings were also organised by a group of Arabs. These Arabs who came, as far as I know, via charitable organisations, and that is why they probably brought with them large amounts of money. I cannot assess what the interests of the HVO at the time was, in letting them into Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I assume that the exclusive motive was to seize money and expensive vehicles from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The closing of communications between Busovaca and Kiseljak before January the 25th, can you say by what events that closure of communications was provoked?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Prior to the 25th of January, 1991, I think that the exact date was the 19th of January, 1991, Dario Kordic was stopped at the checkpoint, as well as Kostroman. As far as I was informed at the time, Dario Kordic threatened to kill the family members of the personnel at the checkpoint. And, as far as I know, Dario Kordic and Kostroman were allowed to pass towards Busovaca. And in the night, between the 20th and the 21st, a terrible incident occurred in Busovaca, when all private shops were blown up by the HVO, and then I think it was on the 21st, or the 22nd, when a part of the units of the HVO started off towards Kacuni, and in front of a roadblock they were stopped. And I think there was an exchange of fire. And then on the 24th, or the night between the 24th and the 25th, a roadblock was put up which could not be opened until I arrived there, together with Bob Stewart, who escorted me, and we opened the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give me just one minute, please. There was a passage of what Colonel Stewart's evidence was said to be that was put to you, and you said you didn't think he could have said that. I am just finding that passage, so that you can have it accurately read over to you. I'll come back to that. And I turn to the next passage of material which was put to you, which was from the Washington Post. You confirmed that a journalist had indeed spoken to you, but the passage that was put to you was based on what other sources were said to have said about you, and the article contained no comment from you on what those other sources had said. First of all, did the journalist, to your recollection, challenge you with what these other sources had said about your being the liaison with foreign Islamic fighters and matters of that sort?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is true that I did give a statement to a journalist of the Washington Post, who came to my office. It is also true that he saw a small Iranian flag, and not a big one, as he reported, in my office. This flag was positioned between a flag of the United States of America and the flag of the Republic of Turkey. In my office, at the time, there were about 25 flags of other countries. These were delegations who officially came to my office and who gave me these flags. The journalist did not report that there's a big Coat of Arms of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in my office and a big Coat of Arms of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in my office --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, I don't want your comments on the article generally, at least I don't. But I do want to know, did the journalist put to you a passage, that was read out by Defence counsel, about your being the liaison with Islamic fighters, and matters of that sort? And if so, did you either accept what he said or did you deny what he said?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is true that the journalist asked me whether I had any connections with the Iranian fighters and the Islamic world. I said I did not have any connection with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will notice that that wasn't set out in the article. One thing that was set out in the article was this, General Merdan: That the journalist says that you said that the names of brigades weren't important, and that you could have a Muslim brigade, a Croat brigade, or a Serb brigade in the new army, so long as they fight for Bosnia. Was the report accurate to that extent?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I did discuss that issue with the journalist, that the name was not important, but the purpose of the brigades who were fighting for the maintenance of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the preservation of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about a passage of Colonel Stewart's evidence. In fact, what happened was he was asked the question, this is page 12371, he was asked by Defence counsel whether he had told General Hadzihasanovic and yourself that they were at least responsible for the outbreak of the fighting that occurred on the 25th of January. And he was asked whether they both agreed, to which he said, in evidence, "I think I certainly told them. Whether they necessarily agreed, I can't remember." He was then asked about a passage in his book "Broken Lives," wherein he recorded an exchange with you, where, in his book a passage was read out. It's at page 12372. And I better read it slowly for your comment. The passage in the book said: "I felt at this time, at least, the Muslims had been responsible for causing much of the trouble by killing two Croat soldiers. Did the Bosnian Muslims really want a full-scale war in the Kiseljak valley? It seemed to me they were going the right way about it. If they did, it was simply not good enough and something must be done. Merdan agreed, apologised, and said he was ready to come himself and try and sort the problem out." Now, that's the full quotation of what was dealt with by Colonel Stewart. Do you have any comment on any of that, as to its accuracy or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Regarding the incident you mentioned, Bob Stewart did visit me, and he blamed me and Hadzihasanovic for interrupting communications. At the time, I realised that the communication had to be opened for a series of reasons, the most important being for the free passage of humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR units. Since at the time I was in contact with Bob Stewart when he blamed us for the barricade, I said that we would lift the barricade. And I asked him to be kind enough to drive me there in his armoured vehicle to the barricade, and I ordered the roadblock to be removed. About half an hour or an hour later, communication was re-established. If Bob said that we were to blame for the all-out conflict in the Lasva Valley -- I don't know all the things that Bob Stewart said, but I think that on the whole, Stewart knows well that we really did try to avoid a conflict, that we did our best to avoid incidents so that a broader conflict would not flare up. And we had discussed this repeatedly, what it would mean for Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to have to fight on two fronts. That did not suit our interest, nor the interest of any single soldier, to have two different fronts. That was what we had discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A very short passage of an exhibit that was not initially produced but was eventually provided, D163/1, was put to you. It's a document -- I'm not going to ask you to look at it again. It's a document dated the 4th of October of 1993. So reporting on the position at that time. The passage which the Chamber, if it wants to find for reference, is on serial number 040225, was that in the area controlled by the 3rd Corps, not a single Croat village had been burnt, according to you, and not a single church destroyed. What do you say about whether you said that and whether that was accurate as at the 4th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that not a single Croatian village had been destroyed and that not a single church had been destroyed either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to go through the artificial exercise of drawing this witness's attentions to other passages of that document, but Chamber will find that the same authors expressed a wide range of views on a number of things, including upon the defendants. And the document has now been produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been suggested to you -- one other document. You were shown a document it's D1A/1. The Chamber will recall it. It's the instructions to the Muslim fighter which originally came to the Chamber in extract but was ultimately provided in full form. You were shown just a couple of extracts from this book or booklet, General. Had you ever seen that book or booklet before? If you remember, it was the instructions to the Muslim fighter, and a couple of pages were put to you about what should be done, whether civilians could be killed and matters of that sort. It was a religious book.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that book for the first time here. I did not have occasion to see those instructions previously given to Muslim fighters. I also said that the author of that book is a highly educated man in religion, and he can interpret religious customs much better than I can. I am a believer, but I said that God knows who is the most faithful believer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any practice of distributing religious booklets or pamphlets to guide soldiers in the BiH Army or not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The fighters of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina of Islamic faith were spoken to by imams about religion. We also made it possible to members of other religions to express their religious feelings. We never prohibited that, and we are not doing so today in the Army of the Federation. I explained to people who asked me about religion that I believe that religion should be present in the army. To what extent the imams managed to distribute such religious materials among fighters, I don't know, but I do know that the imams did profess the faith among believers in the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other questions and one concluding issue. Filipovic, you said, wasn't able to stand up to Kordic. I can't immediately put my finger now on the context, but do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I do, yes, very well. In the beginning of 1992 or, rather, as early as May, late April or early May, Filipovic was with the district staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica. At that time, the commander of the Zenica district Territorial Defence staff was Ramiz Suvalic. Now he's a retired Brigadier, Brigadier-General. And Mr. Ramiz Suvalic and I spoke to Filip Filipovic as we knew that he was an HVO representative from the Lasva Valley or, rather, Central Bosnia. We were talking about setting up a joint command headed by Filip Filipovic, and I would then be his deputy. Mr. Filip Filipovic said that Dario Kordic did not go along with this proposal, and that he could not enforce it. He said he regretted that that was so. And I know that he was removed from that post, because I contacted him repeatedly after that, and for a while he was made a company commander in order to debase him from such a high duty. He was degraded to a company commander. During the fiercest conflicts, I believe he was an operative man in the Operative Zone of the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he explain in any detail why he wasn't able to stand up to Dario Kordic or not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. He did not explain it in detail why he could not stand up to Dario Kordic. He simply said that he disagreed with Dario Kordic's concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been suggested to you that in your evidence you've minimised the real co-operation there was on the ground with the HVO, and I think, by implication, it's been suggested that you were pursuing non-peaceful objectives in the war or warfare that you were, in part, conducting. First of all, have you, in any sense, minimised the co-operation that you actually had with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I never minimised co-operation with the HVO. I always did what I could to establish the co-operation at the highest level, and I was quite ready to subordinate myself; that is, to be Filip Filipovic's deputy. Also that we could stand up to the aggressor against Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I always promoted a reasonable understanding between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, sometimes even against my convictions. I would see some points so that peace could come about. All that my family went through, I never spoke about that because I really desired peace to set in. What the Defence said about how I minimised the possibilities for this is not true. What I also said, HVO military potential was insufficiently or very little used to fight the aggressor against Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Lasva Valley, and elsewhere in Bosnia. I do not know what happened elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've even been asked questions about the commission of war crimes by those with whom you -- with whom you are associated or in respect of whom you may have had authority. Please tell the Chamber this: Have you come here voluntarily? Have you at any stage sought the advantage of protective measures in respect of giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I never asked for any protective measures ever, when I was on the front line or now. I think that truth must triumph, and I'm positive that the truth will triumph and that my life is quite insignificant. I am not afraid for my life, regardless of what will happen in future. I do believe that the truth must come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other questions in re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. General, that concludes your evidence and you are released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. I'm sorry you weren't able to finish it and had to break in the middle, so you had to come twice, but thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should also like to thank you, Mr. President and members of this august Chamber. I was happy to come to testify, and it was an honour for me to be called as a witness. I came of my own free will, and I was quite happy to present the facts and views as I know them. I should also like to thank you for allowing me to comment on some statements on some assertions made here. I do believe that the Tribunal will act upon this and other testimonies and rule as the whole world expects them. Thank you once again for calling me to testify before the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the witness can now leave with the usher, and if we could have a short private session before the next witness, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Pseudonym for this witness will be Witness AD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness AD, for that is the name by which you will be known in these proceedings, please look at this piece of paper, and without reading the name out, confirm that that is your name.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct. That is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have a copy of the summary prepared and served some time ago before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: While the witness is looking at that, Your Honour, we would appreciate that if the Prosecution not lead in respect to paragraph 6. There's also a matter of double or worse hearsay contained in there, 8, 11, 16, and 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. The witness will, in addition to matters referred to in the summary, produce a number of documents, in nearly all cases for very short points of reference. I've got stacks of documents in chronological order that have been provided. No doubt given the proximity of this hearing to the morning break, it will help the Defence to have them all in advance now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I notice the clock is coming up to 11.00, but the witness having just started, we'll go until ten past if that's agreeable to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness AD --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have the Defence had their exhibits? The Defence can have them, of course. And one for the witness himself if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness AD, by background and first occupation, what were you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I served in Her Majesty's forces as a member of the Royal Horse Artillery. I served for eight years as an officer and left in the rank of Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You worked for the ECMM between 1993 and 1995, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Rather than put it at the end as a flourish, I think the position is that for your services in the former Yugoslavia, you were honoured in England; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct. I received an award from Her Majesty the Queen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the MBE, I think, you were given.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, Member of the British Empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1993, were your dealings principally with Blaskic or with Kordic?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: They were principally with Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as Blaskic was concerned, what, if anything, did he say about his authority for places like Zepce and Vares?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: In establishing his area of authority, he explained to me that he was the commander of Operational Zone Middle Bosnia, and that included the brigades in Vares, the Bobovac Brigade, and the brigade in Zepce, also the brigades in Kiseljak, Vitez, and Travnik, although Travnik had then, by this time that I met him, moved to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In general -- we may see reflections of this later in your evidence, but in general, as pockets of Croats became isolated or more firmly isolated, what happened to the authority of people in Blaskic's position?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Well, Blaskic and other commanders became increasingly more physically isolated. They could not move from their locations to all of the pockets. For instance, Blaskic was unable to go to Zepce or to Vares. Therefore, while on paper those brigades were under his command, it was the case that leaders, both political and military in those pockets, began to take authority themselves and increasingly took independent action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did that change the formal lines of authority or not, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It didn't alter the organigramme lines of authority, but certainly it altered the effectiveness of command to actually ensure that their orders were enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with the first sentence of paragraph 5, and the second part of it goes to a later date in the chronology. Was there information about whether the HV were ever involved in the area from time to time?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: There were consistent rumours that HV were involved, and this was, of course, of interest to the leadership both of my mission and those in Vienna -- sorry, Geneva, who are carrying out --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object to any rumours of this type. I don't think that's particularly helpful to the resolution of the issue that's before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Praljak, when did you first meet him and where?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I met General Praljak in March or April. I met him briefly in a field position on the Makljen ridge above Prozor. I then met him later --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. Thank you. Paragraph 6. In June of 1993, were you involved with the evacuation of wounded people from Travnik hospital?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that, how the agreement was made, if there was an agreement, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Having visited the hospital in Travnik, there was a desperate need to evacuate the worst casualties. The situation was particularly bad in the hospital. Therefore, we began, that is, ECMM and the U.N., to try and broker an agreement by which the Muslim and Croat leadership would allow us to evacuate the hospital. This was achieved through meetings with General Blaskic and Dzemal Merdan from the Armija 3rd Corps. So we had a paper commitment that we should be allowed to evacuate from the hospital from Travnik and take the casualties to two hospitals. The Croat casualties would be taken to Nova Bila, and the Muslim casualties would be taken on through to Zenica. The actual coming out of the task though moved more difficulty. Having arranged transport, as we left the Travnik hospital and came to the first Croat checkpoint, the first HVO checkpoint which was at Dolac, we were stopped. We had something like 14 seriously wounded, and I had deliberately selected, although it may be rather callous, that we should have a mixture of people. That would be women, children, men, and also from -- ensuring that we had Croats and Muslims in order that we should be successful and at least alleviate the misery for these individuals. However, at the Dolac checkpoint, we were stopped by the HVO there who refused to let us pass. I began negotiations, making, obviously, reference to the agreement that we had from senior leadership in the Croat community, but this was not going to sway the individuals at the checkpoint. In the course of protracted negotiations, I persuaded the Dolac HVO commander to go back to his leadership, because he had told me he didn't respect the orders of Tihomir Blaskic, he was not -- Blaskic was not his commander. So he left the area. He departed for a long period. We waited. I carried on trying to negotiate, to see if those left at the checkpoint would allow me to pass in the absence of their commander. That, in fact, wasn't the case. The individual, the commander, returned, having seen somebody, I don't know who, and said it would not be possible to allow the whole convoy to go through, although I would be allowed to take just the Croat members of the convoy. I refused to do this. I began negotiations but the situation deteriorated. There were direct threats against the personnel who were with me, and I decided to turn the convoy around and take it back to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness have perhaps map 2781.2 again, the one we've used before. I'm sorry not to have made arrangements to have that made available to him right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that's being produced, Witness AD, was there any evidence available to you of groups which had influence in this particular area? Was there any evidence to whom they were connected?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to the phraseology of that question and the substance of the offer of proof contained in the last part of paragraph 6 there. It appears that the evidence is double hearsay, at least, from people who were apparently employed by the witness, not monitors but, rather, others, I believe. I think in the absence of a better foundation, this sort of rumour-type evidence is particularly damaging, so we object to it under Rule 89(C) and (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Lay the foundation, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with it in two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all -- let the witness see if he can find the checkpoint. When he's placed the checkpoint, if he could lay it on the ELMO for us. Lay it on the ELMO. The usher will show you how we use the ELMO. I'm sorry you haven't had an opportunity to look at the courtroom before coming in.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: We need to see that part of map. Okay. Do I point on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. If you point out there, we can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Travnik is off the map. It's off the left-hand edge of the map, the road leading from Travnik down to Vitez [indicates]. There is a junction where a road diverts north and leads by circuitous route to Zenica. This was known us to as the Dolac checkpoint, and it was just to the west of that road that I met the HVO checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The question I previously asked you I'll break in to two parts. Just yes or no: Was there evidence of the influence of groups -- don't name the groups -- operating in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's the whole point, evidence. And I hate -- I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think that that's not the proper way to lay the foundation. We need to know what it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- what court documents, what monitors, what reliable sources were consulted or relied upon by the witness in concluding that that was evidence of a connection with these groups that we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To that I'm coming, and I'm quite happy to do it by the other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In relation to any groups having authority there, was this something you knew yourself or something that was told to you by others?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I knew that there were elements belonging loosely to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you know about it? Before we hear what you're going to tell us about it, how did you learn about it? Did you learn about it from what you did yourself and from seeing people there, from talking to people?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: There were certain locations where we saw groupings of armed individuals, often quite well equipped, often wearing the same uniform, which was not the case throughout the whole of the HVO. They naturally drew our attention to inquire as to who these individuals were. And the names of two groups --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you make a break between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- what was distinctive about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a complaint by the interpreters; no break between question and answer. Could you bear in mind, Witness AD, that everything is having to be interpreted --

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and slow down if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Entirely my fault, and my apologies are due to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What uniforms, what distinctive uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It wasn't so much the distinctiveness of the uniform but the fact that they were all wearing the same uniform. In some areas, you would find that the HVO may possibly -- an individual would be wearing combat trousers but a civilian top. As the month progressed uniform became more established, but in the early times it was clear that not everybody had access to uniforms. However, there were some groups that appeared to be better equipped and better uniformed than others and seemed to have a coherence about them that was lacking in some of the HVO units. Those, naturally, were of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these groups, yes just yes or no, known by a particular name or names?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you learn the names? Don't tell us the names. How did you learn the names?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: We learnt the names through inquiry, through inquiries with locals, and also through my contacts with the UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the soldiers themselves ever tell you their name or use their names?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No. Not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there consistency in the information coming to you from the different sources you spoke of as to the names of the groups?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next separate part of the same general issue: Did -- just yes or no. Did information come to you, or did you become aware of any connection between these groups and any particular individual? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again without naming individuals, what was the means by which that information came to you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Through inquiry with locals, sometimes through cross-checking with our contacts with the Armija forces, in any way that we could sort of triangulate to get information about the names, the make-up, and who these people worked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who are these locals?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was that addressed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who were these locals, Witness AD?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: The locals were typically staff employed by us. These were of varied background, some Croats, some Muslims, some Montenegrins, and some Slovenians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What tasks, if more than one, were these locals doing for you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Interpreting, driving, general administration. They were one source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's admissible. Yes, we'll admit this. I take it, there is no dispute about the fact that these groups were operating locally? No dispute about that, Mr. Sayers, presumably? The dispute is about the second part of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's exactly right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will admit it, in any event, having heard the background. And then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I just ask you for the detail, one other question. The information coming to you from the various sources about the person to whom these groups were connected, did that have consistency about it or not?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then, please, the name of the groups and the person to whom they were connected?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: The groups were known as the Jokers and the Apostoli, and the person that was most often connected was Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, on this topic, at the time that you were there, and apart from Blaskic and Kordic, was there any other local leader of whom you were aware to whom Blaskic could have turned or any other local commander could have turned for guidance or authority?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Not located within Central Bosnia, but there was a chain of command outside of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn. Half an hour, please. By that clock, quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 7. It may be desirable for the witness to have Exhibit 1031, which has already been produced. It's not in the stack. 1031. While that's being produced, is it right that on the 8th or 9th of June you visited an area north of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We know, and the Chamber has already seen, that Mr. Morsink prepared a report in relation to that. Did you have a view at that time as to the reality, understatement or overstatement, of atrocities alleged by Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croat leadership had suggested that there had been mass ethnic cleansing, atrocities committed, and desecration of cultural sites. We had difficulty getting access to the area, but in order to try and determine validity of their claims, we entered into negotiation with Armija, and I succeeded in getting through to villages around Brajkovici, an area between Guca Gora and Zenica. We visited the church there and found that the church was in good order. There had been no desecration, although there was no members of the Croat population left. Clearly, everyone had left the village. But the destruction was in the form of looting and not of destruction of houses. Our overall assessment on that visit and visits to other villages, I am thinking of the area around Dolac and also Guca Gora itself, that the claims of destruction were exaggerated. But clearly there had been large movements of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber has Exhibit 1031 before it, as does the witness, it can remind itself that the broad summary on page 1 was prepared by (redacted) (redacted). This witness's entry, starting at page 2 of the document, and in paragraph 1 of page 2, Witness AD, did you refer in particular to the village of Ovcarevo, that's five lines up from the bottom, of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that village was deserted, being looted by Armija. Then you went on to say that the -- a further report that the Croat village of Dolac was deserted and over 100 houses burnt. You did say there was evidence of some houses still burning?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Third and last page under "comment," you set out there that the movement of Croat civilians -- I apologise to the interpreters. I suspect this document is not before them. And it can't, I'm afraid, be placed on the ELMO because of the witness protection. I'll read these four lines very slowly: "The movement of Croat civilians to the area of Vitez and subsequently to Busovaca and Novi Travnik is large and significant. The reasons for the move are less clear but appear to relate to a wildly voiced belief that Mujahedin forces were committing atrocities. When investigated, evidence was not found." And was it your position that there was some evacuation of Croat villages brought about by allegations of Mujahedin atrocities?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, it was clear to us, particularly in the village of Ovcarevo, that the movement of the Croat population had been organised. In the case of Ovcarevo, they actually moved north through Serbian lines, which was of interest to us, because it demonstrated contacts and a degree of trust in relationship with the Serbs. In other areas, particularly the villages I mentioned earlier, between Guca Gora and Zenica, it appeared that the population had moved prior to the fighting, which is possibly -- well, is definitely understandable. But we believe that in some cases the population was told to move. The reasons for them being told to move was because it was often voiced to us that the Mujahedin would carry out atrocities, and therefore the population should leave before that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 I deal with really by one question only, in light of the considerable quantity of material already presented. At the Tuzla convoy incident, on the 11th of June, by whom on the Croat side was the problem resolved?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: The problem was resolved by direct negotiations with Dario Kordic. Tihomir Blaskic was also involved. He had given the initial guarantees of movement, but those had clearly broken down, and Jean-Pierre Thebault entered into direct negotiations with Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 9, and the first of the exhibits in the stack, the small stack I have to say. This will become Exhibit 1076.1, and is a Travnik special report of the 19th of June, prepared by you and one other. And we can see on the second sheet at page -- paragraph 4, where you set out that Guca Gora set a pattern that was to recur in all future allegations. The first was large scale ethnic cleansing, the second was mass destruction, the third were widespread atrocities. And then you set out the inquiry and something about population movements. Do you want to comment further on that?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Well, I simply stated that the inquiry into Guca Gora set the pattern that, first, the population moves had occurred but often in suspicious circumstances. By that I mean that it appeared that the Croat leadership had ordered the evacuation of the villages prior to the actual combat. I also stated that the war damage to houses was minimal, and that we had not, at that time, found any proof of atrocities. My final comment was that press reports appeared to be grossly exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit in the bundle, I think, is the 17th of August. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This picks up from something that you said earlier. Under paragraph 2, this being a daily summary of yours, rather than just read the paragraph there, summarise its effects for the Chamber, please, with reference to General Praljak and who he was.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I met General Praljak in a long meeting. I note here it says around about two hours. We discussed his position and the situation in the area in which he was operating. General Praljak had served with the HV forces in Vukovar. I believe that his background is actually one of an actor rather than military, but he had, by reputation, established himself as a capable soldier, and he was, at this time, commanding the forces in the area of Prozor, although he claimed that he had, in fact, assumed a much wider responsibility but saw that his need was to be where, at that time, the action was, which was on the Prozor-Gornji Vakuf front. I asked about his background, having served with the HV, and also about allegations and persistent reports that we had of HV involvement. General Praljak denied that there were any HV forces operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but did state that individuals like himself, who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina, had returned, seeing it was their duty to fight for the Croat cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the passage in your report that we've looked at in general, the reference to the HV stopping at nothing to defeat the Muslims, including the blocking of all aid during the winter and cutting off water supplies, and then there's reference further down to -- that if the valleys could not be won back by negotiations, then a military alliance with the Serbs would be formed and they would be retrieved by force and so on. Are these quotations or inferences or what?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: This is what he -- this is my interpretation of what he said. I mean, I haven't put it in quotation marks, but it was clear to me that this was his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My shortcoming not to have asked already that all exhibits will be under seal, please. I'm grateful to the registrar for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please 1176.2, the last one having been 1172.2. This exhibit, Witness AD, is one you first saw recently, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's another report of which you have a memory, which we've been trying to find, so far unsuccessfully, which is referred to in the summary. One part of this particular document chimes with your recollection of that other report, I think, but --

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Well, the -- I had a meeting with Dario Kordic sometime at the end of August, and this particular exhibit is dated 21st of August. So this meeting here was before the one I recollect, but for some reason there is no ability to retrace the special report. The reason I went to see Mr. Kordic was because there had been a shelling incident in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a minute. Are you dealing with this report? I would like you to deal with this report first.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Right. In the case --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to the other report in due course.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: In the case of this report, it was clear from what I've written that I was having a general meeting with him, discussing command structures, seniorities, cross-checking with information that I'd had from other sources, including my meeting with General Praljak. I made an assessment towards the end that Dario Kordic appeared to be out of touch. My feeling during that meeting was that he had not displayed necessarily the stature of a politician of his seniority. I gained the impression that he seemed to be rather isolated. That, to a certain extent, may have been something to do with the surroundings in which we had the meeting. I went to Mr. Kordic's lodge, which was near Busovaca and fairly isolated in itself. But I gained the impression that I was hearing -- reading from a script which really didn't bear much reality to what was going on on the ground, and I felt that he was rather out of touch and believing his own propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see from your report of the 21st of August that he blamed General Merdan as the main war criminal.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He made an assessment of HVO capability, which you regarded as unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes. And this led me to make my conclusion at the end that he was out of touch, because there was a suggestion during this meeting that the HVO would regain territory that they had lost and link the Kiseljak pocket with Vares and also the Zepce pockets. This was very unrealistic. At that time, the HVO had been very much on the defensive and had shown no ability whatsoever to take offensive action, particularly across the distances that were being discussed here. It seemed not to be the assessment of someone who really had a grasp on the military realities. But I accept that he had a position and a statement to make, and that's what he said to me, but it wasn't realistic with what could be achieved by the HVO forces at that time on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He did give you an order of military seniority going Boban, Praljak, Petkovic, Tole, and Martic?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes. General Praljak's arrival in territory had created a question of his seniority to General Petkovic, who was the commander of the HVO, and Petkovic's record had not been particularly good, certainly seen from outside of Central Bosnia. His forces had lost territory, and General Praljak's arrival seemed to be in some way a replacement. So I was keen to establish what the orders of seniority were. And as stated in my report, Dario Kordic said that the order was Boban, Praljak, Petkovic, Tole, and Martic. Tole had been an officer, I believe in command of forces in Travnik, but I might stand corrected there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn from this document, we should look at paragraph 8, which I forecast earlier when dealing with the developing isolation of areas in pockets, because you make some comments there, which we don't need to go into extensively, but I draw them to everyone's attention for their assistance, about the feeling of isolation displayed by the Vares HVO command, who previously stated they suppose they came under the command of Blaskic more than anyone else.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And this reinforces what was stated earlier, that the isolation of the pockets meant that the commanders didn't have much information about what was going on in those pockets. They certainly had some, and there was other evidence that they had links with those pockets but not the ability to visit them. They were always very keen, because the organisation that I was with had good access, to find out what was happening in those pockets as an organisation that wasn't delivering anything other than information and the ability to give individuals a chance to say and state their position. We often traded information for access. Therefore, when we met people such as Dario Kordic and Colonel Blaskic, they were very, very keen to have our impression of the actual situation on the ground in those pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A quick look at the next Exhibit 1178,1, dated the 23rd of August. At this time, if we look at paragraph 8, "Assessment" first, we see your comments: "The lack of any publicised map on the Geneva proposal is almost farcical." Perhaps that provides the setting. And you make the point that the detail that is available is that Vares and Zepce have become under Muslim jurisdiction. And so when we come back to paragraph 2, "Political Activity," the reference to somebody meeting Pejcinovic, is that you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No, this is one of my team's, Victor 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But they reported back to you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I was in -- I was the office to whom they reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see that at that stage there was bitter recrimination about the future of Vares, as decided in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next Exhibit 1185,3, for the 28th of August. A report of yours. And at the foot of the first sheet. This was, I think, a meeting with you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, this was. And I had taken the Deputy Head of the regional centre, who was a new appointee, to try and introduce him to some of the key personalities in the area. And I spoke to Colonel Blaskic and asked him about the Geneva proposals, which, as stated in the previous Z1178,1, was causing enormous confusion on the ground, as to what was being discussed in Geneva and the implications on the ground. And when I asked Colonel Blaskic about these, he stated that Dario Kordic spoke on the matters concerning ideas, while he dealt with the reality. I went on to make a comment, that: "Dario Kordic is the key HDZ political figure in Central Bosnia, and has long been suspected of controlling the HVO. It is assessed that his influence over Blaskic is significant, if not total." May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's on that topic, yes.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It is on the topic, but it relates to the previous Z1178, the visit of Victor 3 to Vares. That Victor 3 was given a letter by the mayor of Vares concerning these Geneva proposals, and the suggestion that Vares was to come under Muslim control. He gave this to ECMM.
