utterances.text: All right. In fact, sir, I think it's true that you never saw or heard Colonel Blaskic actually consulting Mr. Kordic specifically before making a military decision of his own; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I think that also, to be fair, you did refer to one occasion upon which Mr. or Colonel Blaskic said that he needed to have consultations before making a particular decision, and I don't particularly remember what context that was in. But you do not know whether he consulted his commanding officer within the military chain of command to make that decision, do you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It was about access to Stari Vitez. No, I don't know to whom he referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fine. Just one question about Colonel Siljeg, to whom you referred in your testimony. He was the Colonel Blaskic figure, if you like, the commander of the northwest Herzegovina operative zone while you were in Gornji Vakuf; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of -- and based in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And there is no question that he was the senior military commander in that region either; is there, sir?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No. That was the person to whom we had all our dealings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say, sir, that there was no suggestion that Mr. Kordic had to be consulted before decisions were made in the Gornji Vakuf area?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In other words, his political influence didn't extend down as far as Gornji Vakuf, as far as you were able to tell?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It's difficult to -- unlike a military situation where people do have defined boundaries, I'm not sure how one defines the boundaries of political responsibility. But certainly operational zone, middle Bosnia, which Blaskic was commanding, did not include Bugogno or Gornji Vakuf, and I made reference to or had to make reference to any of the dealings in that valley to Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one more question in that regard, although not that particular area. The same would be true of your time in Mostar. Mr. Kordic's political influence certainly didn't extend to military matters in Mostar, did it sir?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: There would appear to be more senior leadership in Mostar, and they probably made the decisions, rather than referring to the isolation of Mr. Kordic in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some pretty graphic testimony, Witness AD, regarding the -- your perception of the increasing isolation of the Croat pockets that were left as the summer of 1993 went on. I think it's true that the Croats were squeezed into four pockets, essentially, the Vitez-Busovaca pocket first; second, the Zepce pocket; third, the Kiseljak pocket; and fourth, the Vares pocket. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take it, sir, that your perception was that the isolation increased with the passage of time, with the increasing success of the Muslim offensive in the summer of 1993 against the Croat forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so your report regarding that perception of isolation in August of 1993, would certainly be even more accurate as of late October of 1993, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, the isolation and freedom of movement was increasingly more difficult. And the position of certain pockets, particularly at the time that I moved from Central Bosnia to Mostar, was critical. The Vares pocket being the most critical. The Zepce pocket was very much more secure, but for different reasons. Certain allegiances and alliances and agreements had been reached with the Serbian forces in that area, and their position was much less tenuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning just to the Vares pocket for one moment, sir. A considerable degree of frustration had been expressed to you by the political and military leadership in Vares, expressing to you, I think, as of August of 1993, expressing to you the view that they had essentially been cut adrift by the Croat political leadership; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I would say that they have -- their main concern was what was going on in Geneva, that they were going to be sold out, their territory would be handed over. Again, referring to one of the documents produced this morning. We were given by the mayor this letter, saying that they felt -- to be addressed to their leadership. That they felt that they were being let down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And one final question in that regard. You gave some testimony regarding trading access for information. Would it be fair to say that all of the Croat leadership that you interviewed, both political and military, were always hungry for information about an isolated area, such as Vares?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. And it was also true of the Muslim leadership, wanting to know what was happening to their isolated minority communities. It was the only tool we had with which to carry out our work, was utilising that need for information. And, obviously, we never passed anything sensitive or anything military, but certainly, in the case of Vares, I do remember discussing with General Blaskic the civilian situation, and their fears and anxieties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that, from Colonel Blaskic's perspective, it was difficult to get information about the situation of Croats in Vares, just as it was for the Muslims to get accurate information about the situation of the residents of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, it was difficult. But there was certainly some communication between the two. I do remember seeing a data transmission sheet, which I assume had been a satellite system of communication between Zepce and the HVO headquarters. So there was ability to communicate, but not ability to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Sorry. If I could add one extra bit. There was the ability, at a later stage, and I would allude to the period from roughly beginning of August, where people in the Kiseljak pocket were able to move, and, in fact, anywhere where there was a Croatian community that had a front line with Serbian authorities. The difficult situation and the isolation of Croat pockets led them, as I said in the case of Zepce, to agreements, and also in the case of Vares. So it would have been physically possible for some people who have moved from Kiseljak to Vares, but getting, for instance, from Busovaca to Kiseljak was difficult if not impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me just turn to one of the subjects that the Presiding Judge raised; the Jokers. The Trial Chamber has already heard extensive evidence concerning the command and control of this unit, which was a sub-unit of the military police. Did you ever actually yourself speak to any of the military police commanders in Vitez? First let me ask you about Mr. Zvonko Vukovic, who was the commander of the military police until January 19, 1993, I believe. Do you ever remember speaking with him, sir?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I don't recall the names. I certainly met the leadership, both -- and then it changed, and I'm trying very hard. Somebody, it wasn't Petar, but his successor, I also met him briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is not a memory contest, sir. Let me just suggest to you the names and this may jog your memory. Do you recall that Pasko Ljubicic became the chief of the military police, the 4th Battalion of the military police, headquartered in Vitez from January the 19th, 1993 until the end of July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: The exact dates -- I don't know the name now. I do recall. But I must say at the time I may not have made a distinction between the fact that he was military police. He was just the head of the police, as far as I was concerned, and most of the dealings with him would have been at my team level, which would have been Victor 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that as far as you're aware -- well, as far as you're aware, the ECMM generated no reports whatsoever concerning the command or control structure of this Jokers sub-unit of the military police?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any special reports being written, and I did not give any -- as a task to any of my teams to discover more about that structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, sir. And I take it that it follows from that that you yourself never wrote any reports on that subject?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I may well have mentioned them as their names and being present at certain places but I don't ever recall writing a special report, whereas I do recall writing special reports about Mujahedin, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And the same goes for the other group that you mentioned, the Apostoli, I believe. Is it your recollection that that group was located in Kiseljak and was supposed to be affiliated particularly with the gentleman that you mentioned, Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I don't remember their location, to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Suffice it to say though, sir, to hand you haven't been shown any notes or memoranda, contemporaneous memoranda or anything that you wrote in connection with either these Jokers sub-unit or the Apostoli contingent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct, and they may -- as I say, they may well have been mentioned as part of a report, but I definitely did not write any special reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And just so we finish up this, you never spoke to any Joker or Apostle yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Well, I understand that the leadership was the policeman to whom we've referred and I spoke to them. So the answer is yes, I did speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever speak to Marinko Palavra, who was the chief of police following Pasko Ljubicic, from August 1st, 1993 up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I can't recall. I'm sure if he was a key leader then I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: None of these gentlemen, Mr. Vukovic, Mr. Ljubicic, or Mr. Palavra said that they had -- were subordinate to or had to take the orders of Mr. Kordic, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I don't remember asking that specific question, so you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to the source of information that you gave about this connection. I think you described it as being, between Mr. Kordic and these two groups. Do you know what the source of information used by your interpreters or drivers or the other locals that you spoke to was? You don't, do you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Well, I do -- as I said this morning, we never rely on one source, and so most of my information on these groups and their linkage would have come from UNPROFOR. The statements made by our interpreters were just their opinion on who these people were and who they reported to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when you say "UNPROFOR," Witness AD, what you're referring to is the British Battalion component of UNPROFOR at Bila; correct? They're the people with whom you principally dealt?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: They're the people with whom I principally dealt, but you remember that the UNPROFOR component organisation in that area included other nationalities, the Dutch based in Busovaca, the Belgians, and we always utilised the national connections we had in ECMM. So my personal contact would have been with the BritBat, but we would not have relied on that exclusively. What was of interest to these groups was that things happened at times when we had agreement of the official HVO command structure, but things didn't happen because of the interventions of others, so we wanted to know to whom these others reported. And the consistent belief and understanding was there were groups who were outside of Mr. Blaskic's command who were under the authority of Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But your basis for that was really upon all of this secondhand information that you were receiving from other people, and you don't really know what their information was based on, do you, sir? That's fair to say, I believe.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I think it would be fair to say that all my information in the ECMM fell into that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Let's move on. Just to return to the time when you came back into the Travnik -- or came up to the Travnik area for the first time, was this the first time that you actually had any dealings with events in Central Bosnia, sir, when you came up in the first week of June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No. I had been up to the headquarters of Mr. Blaskic on an earlier inquiry into individuals, particularly Croats, who were being abducted on the route between Gornji Vakuf and Travnik. There had been several disappearances. Initially exclusively Croat community. And as part of trying to resolve what was happening, I remember taking Mr. Zrinko Tokic, who was the commander of the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf, up to Central Bosnia and meeting various people en route. We stopped and actually spoke to the Armija in Opara, a village along that route, and I went to Central Bosnia in that capacity. That was my one recollection. I also went up to a social function. So I went a couple of times into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But it would be fair to say that your principle concentration was Gornji Vakuf, the Gornji Vakuf area, and you didn't hold yourself out as an expert in the Travnik-Vitez-Busovaca area at the time that you went up to Travnik in the first week of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And when you arrived in the first week of June, that was immediately before the beginning of the summer offensive by the ABiH forces in the Travnik area; correct?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It was the beginning of the fighting between the Croats and the Armija, which later turned into something of an offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That offensive was also launched on a second prong, if you like, in Kakanj area, was it not? Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but it had also happened prior to Travnik, in the area around Zenica, when the Croatian brigade that was in Zenica, in fact, under the command, I believe, of Mr. Tolic [sic] --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Totic, yes. I'm sorry. ECMM had been involved in securing his release. So it had happened in Zenica. We then had an attempt to put out the fire in Travnik. That failed. Then later there were offences in Kakanj area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, in April of 1993, your understanding is the HVO sources in Zenica had been defeated and essentially the military HVO presence in Vitez had been expunged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. What initiated that fighting and the reasons why it took place, of course, is a broader question of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand, sir. And then in June, the military presence of the HVO in Travnik was expunged as a result of military defeats suffered by the HVO at the hands the ABiH and, similarly, almost simultaneously, the HVO was being defeated in Kakanj as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, but there was a gap between what was happening in Kakanj and what happened in Travnik. But I think it's true to say that really starting in the north of the Lasva Valley, sorry, north-west of the Lasva Valley in Travnik. Fighting moved further south down to Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just so that we have an idea for the total numbers of displaced persons or refugees, do you have an estimate of the total number of refugees that were generated as a result of the Travnik offensive? We've heard numbers ranging from 5.000 to 20.000. What would be a fair number of the Croats that were expelled from their homes as a result of that offensive, sir?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I would say it was nearer the 20.000 more than the 5.000. I do recall more accurately the numbers of people who remained in Travnik and other areas such as Bugojno, which was somewhere between two, two and a half, and 4.000 initially, but that, in the case of Travnik, depleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you have an estimate or did the ECMM have an estimate as to the number of displaced persons and refugees expelled from their homes as a result of the Kakanj offensive? We've heard numbers of 15.000. Does that sound broadly accurate?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I honestly can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And --

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It was significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One final question. In the later months, in August and September, I believe, there was another offensive in the area from which you've just come, Bugojno. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I recall it very clearly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you recall that there was an atrocity committed at Uzdol, I believe, in September of 1993, involving 35 Croats who were executed?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, although I must say I was in England at the time. But it certainly occurred, and we did have ECMM presence. My team in Gornji Vakuf went to the site and, I believe, took the BBC. It was well documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether any formal investigations were started by the ABiH and whether any people were brought to justice or any military commanders removed from their command as a result of that massacre, sir?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any formal inquiry, investigation, and I don't remember any changes of leadership because of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were taken very briefly through the so-called Convoy of Joy, sir, and you'll be happy to know that I'm not going to ask you any questions on that, because we've heard a lot of that already. Turning to the detailed meetings that you described in your direct-examination, one of the meetings that you had with Mr. Kordic was on September the 1st of 1993. Do you recall that? And that was the -- where you said that there was a discussion about a shelling incident.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It was around that time. I'm not sure that it was September the 1st, but it was certainly around there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. We actually -- we have an ECMM document dated September the 1st, 1993. I'm the first to say that it's somewhat elliptical, but let me see if it can jog your memory, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And we'd like this as the next Defence exhibit, please. And just for the witness's information and the Trial Chamber's information, I'm going to do my level best to finish up this examination in about ten minutes if I can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked D165/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And we'll try to get you out of here, Witness AD. This document, sir, is a daily summary prepared by the regional centre in Zenica. There's a reference on page 2, paragraph 3, to the HRC and DHRC having a long meeting with Mr. Kordic, who is identified as the vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, and they both express very clear views about the future according to this summary, and a special report was to be prepared the next day. Is the DHRC you?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No. I believe -- I don't believe -- this is not the meeting to which I went. I believe this was Jean-Pierre Thebault, and the deputy -- I can't remember who it was at the time. I don't believe this is the meeting that I was at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Witness AD, that document need detain us no further. Thank you. I'm through with it. Just a few final matters. You gave some testimony about spotting vehicles with Hrvatska Voijska marks on the side or HV, and people dressed in uniforms bearing HV insignia. Did you ever speak to any of them?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No, I didn't speak to any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And, in fact, it's true, is it not, that the existence and extent of HV involvement had always been difficult to define in your view, involvement in Central Bosnia or south-western Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that many of the ABiH reports regarding alleged spottings of HV troops were seldom confirmed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It was an area of continued interest. What was different about this sighting was the quantity and quality, and my personal sighting. This was a professional unit. This was unlike anything in my years' experience in ECMM that I had seen of the HVO. This was well equipped, good equipment, large scale. This was something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I understand. Would it be fair to say, though, that in all the time that you spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was the only time that you ever spotted troops that you concluded were HV troops?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: On this scale, yes. I mean, I certainly saw individuals, but there was no way of confirming -- who were wearing HV insignia. There was no way of confirming whether they were there just as volunteers or as a unit. That was the only time I saw anything on this scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you do anything to try to find out where these troops were going, what they were doing, what their mission was or did you just leave it up in the air?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No. No. This was a very interesting, and I wrote a special report. You will note that the date was sort of middle of January, and you'll know that I left in early February. But I did see this with the head of the regional centre at the time, Sir Martin Garrod, who was travelling down to Herzegovina with me. So we wrote this special report, and it was then -- became part of the team's responsibility covering that area, which was Mike 4, to find out where these were going. I mean, clearly they couldn't have gone any further than Prozor at the time, but it was something which I believe that the head of the regional centre would have continued investigating after my departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, though, that you don't know whether he did, in fact, continue those investigations, and if he did, what the results of those investigations were, if any?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct. I don't know whether he definitely did continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So the conclusion is that you yourself do not know what these troops were doing, what their mission was, where they were going, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No. I think that's an overstatement. They were on one road. That one road only led to Prozor. They were going in the opposition direction to me. They were going into Central Bosnia. I had not seen anything like it. I had been serving in the military myself. I had some understanding of what I was seeing here was different, as I said, to anything I'd seen before. And there seems to be no major attempt, with the exception of removing number plates, to disguise the fact that this was something coming from outside. I could not be more definite -- this was an HV unit -- short of interrogating individual soldiers in some way, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You never saw any HV units, though, in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket or anywhere in Central Bosnia during your time (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just two final areas, sir. Your meeting with Colonel Blaskic after the war, he actually informed you that Ivica Rajic had been removed from command and would be punished as a result of his activities during the war, did he not?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Can you jog my mind as to when this meeting happened? Was this when Mr. Blaskic had assumed the command of the HVO and replaced Mr. Roso?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I can't honestly recall that, but I'd be prepared to -- it's a likely sort of question that I would have asked because of what happened in Stupni Do and the various allegations as to who was involved there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. One final question in connection with your meeting with Mr. Kordic in November of 1994. He never said anything to intimate to you that in his view the Croats were not committed to the development of the Federation of Croats and Muslims that resulted from the peace agreement, in fact, quite the reverse. He told you that the Croats were committed to the development of the Federation, did he not?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is true. He told me they were committed. And I asked evidence of that commitment, pointed to the disparities between what he was stating and what might be achieved if he were to send the signal to the International Community that they were. But he certainly did not give me any other indication, other than that the Croats were supporting the Federation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: -- have been embarrassed by some of the questions I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He told you that these were tough things to achieve, that small steps were necessary, and that those small steps were being taken towards the ultimate goal, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, sir. I have no further questions, unless the Trial Chamber has any for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Cerkez Defence has no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few matters arising, Witness AD. The Mostar delegates, generally, just help us with this. Were they, in any sense, elected or were they appointed to their positions?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: There were no elections held. They were appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked questions about military as opposed to political function. First, in relation to Stari Vitez. In your judgement, was there any need for a matter of that scale and at that location to be referred outside of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I don't think that the -- anyone outside of Central Bosnia would have been particularly familiar -- well, they would have been familiar, but I don't think they would have been consulted. I think this was something that would have been sorted out within the leadership, within Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And within Central Bosnia, no one superior to Blaskic on the military chain. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Within Central Bosnia, that is correct. Although, it might be that Mr. Kordic, with equal rank, in military rank, may have at times sought military intervention, but primarily Mr. Kordic was dealing with the political side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, generally, where a military man doesn't make a decision himself but refers elsewhere, if he is simply referring upwards in a military line of command, or chain of command, is there any reason for him not to say so, that you can think of?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But, in Blaskic's case, when he referred matters elsewhere, did he ever volunteer where he was referring matters to?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Mostar military leaders, you were asked some questions about them, and about Kordic's involvement or not, so far as they were concerned. But just this: Are you saying, in one way or another, that the Mostar military leaders did or didn't have political influence or control to which they were subject?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I believe that the professional elements within the military would defer to the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Mostar, were there political leaders at a level senior to that of Kordic, in your judgement or not? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, there would be political leaders senior to Kordic. For instance, Mr. Boban and Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about the source of information of interpreters, drivers, and so on. You spoke of how you relied on SFOR but also gathered information from your interpreters and drivers. Speaking generally, are you able to help us with where the interpreters and drivers said they got their information, or was it too general or too varying for you to be able to specify?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It was pretty general.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As between interpreters, drivers, and SFOR, which was your principle source of information, if one? Put another way, which was the subordinate source of information, if one?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to give the impression that we didn't do our own investigations on things generally. So, UNPROFOR would have been a point of reference. And if I had to state with which spoke with most authority about military matters, without a shadow of a doubt it would have been UNPROFOR and not a reliance on local staff's interpretation or interpretation of, for instance, Armija commanders. It would have all been cross-referenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in the event, did you find consistency between the sources of information?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: However many it was trucks that you saw going to Prozor, marked in the way you've described, in your experience, would that movement have to be documented?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The state from which it came and even in the state to which it went, if it was passing into a different state?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: It would have been documented at a military organisation level. Whether it was documented because it was crossing into another state -- when the borders of the Croat dominated territory of Bosnia was linked to that of Croatia, I'm not sure about political contacts or clearance, but certainly there would be military -- you don't carry out a movement of that scale without there being military orders and documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, such movement would have to be supported by fuel and by food and all sorts of other things of a comparatively mundane type?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Absolutely. There's an administrative tale to these movements, and that would have been the case in this particular observation of these HV movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the assumption that those vehicles came from Croatia, which is what you are saying in your evidence, documents will exist showing the real, or at least the stated purpose of those, or would have existed, showing the real or stated purpose of that movement?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: Yes, they would have. Whether they still exist, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Ivicia Rajic, do you have actually any recollection of the conversation with Blaskic about him?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: No. It's a topic I may have discussed. I don't recall discussing it with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Therefore, you recall -- do you recall anything about whether he was punished, whether he returned from punishment, anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: AD
utterances.text: I mean, I do have some vague recollection of discussing it, but I honestly can't give you any more detail than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes what I want to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness AD, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. And you are now released. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, unless there is something anybody wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know the difficulties of dealing with administrative matters with a protected witness present. There are just two things I can say, and I can deal with them without his leaving. As to the possibility of a video-link, I think I've opted for the other course, at least for the time being. I'll speak to the witness concerned and, providing I can be sure he will be here before our case may end, however early that may be. They are not going to take us until the 10th of March, if I can possibly deal with it earlier than that, although I think that may be very difficult. So, for the time being not him. There has been a skeleton argument filed in relation to one witness, for whom a skeleton had already been filed. In relation to the other witness, the skeleton that I would serve is no more than I've already put on the transcript. I've extracted the transcript, and there are copies of the extract that will be made available to my learned friends and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And trying to make sure that we are ahead of problems, the Defence have indicated to us, in respect of a witness who gave evidence in Blaskic on the 8th of December, 1997, protected witness, that they require his attendance. If we are now -- we are not in private session, are we? We are just in open session. I'm not sure that they are in a position to require it, as it's a witness for whom there is testimony in another case. It may be a matter that could again be usefully ventilated this week. I don't require -- I don't seek to have skeletons. I can deal with the matter as it is raised. But it might be useful to look at that as something else that we can deal with this week, if by chance we run out of evidence, and we can deal with that. Similarly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll just interrupt you there. We may need a copy of that transcript, if you want us to rule upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'll make inquiries with your legal officer, to ensure that that happens. Similarly, speaking somewhat elliptically, there is outstanding an application effectively to call as an additional witness a superior in position and rank to the last witness but one. Indeed, he was referred to. There was objection taken to that witness. I'm not sure that he is going to be asking for any protection, but I am speaking elliptically, just in case he does. Again, can we deal with that issue, if it turns up this week. In that case, a statement and an unsigned statement was served, along with a transcript of evidence, he being a witness who was called by another Chamber. He wasn't called by a party. And so again it -- although we may want that witness for only a very small amount of evidence, it may be that the Chamber will want to either have access to or at least know where to find the material that's available in relation to him. That's probably all I need raise now, to keep things moving and to avoid time being wasted later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Half past 9 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
